title: When a critical vulnerability hits, do you know where you’re exposed?
summary: When a critical vulnerability hits, the hard part is knowing where you’re exposed. See how discovery, CMDB context and automation speed remediation.
body_markdown:
Security teams might know that a vulnerability exists. IT operations teams might know that patches are available. But if neither team has an accurate, current picture of where the vulnerable technology is running, remediation becomes a time-consuming investigation before a single system gets patched.


Speed alone isn’t the answer either. Effective vulnerability management means a controlled process aligned with operational requirements and change policies, rather than pushing every available update everywhere as quickly as possible. That process depends on knowing what’s affected, what depends on it and what to fix first.


## **PHP2Shell: a critical vulnerability with a visibility problem**


The recently disclosed PHP vulnerabilities[CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619](https://cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisories/al26-026-critical-vulnerabilities-impacting-php-cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619) , collectively known as PHP2Shell, show why knowing where vulnerable software runs matters as much as having the patch. Rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale, they can enable unauthenticated remote code execution in affected PHP environments. Security researchers have reported exploitation attempts in the wild, and the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added both flaws to its[Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog?field_cve=CVE-2026-109618) . Patched PHP releases, including 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, became available on October 21, 2026.


On the surface, the response seems straightforward: identify affected systems and patch them. In a complex enterprise environment, that “identify” step can be far more difficult than it sounds.


PHP may be running across physical and virtual servers, cloud workloads, legacy applications and other parts of a hybrid IT estate. Knowing which business applications an organization operates doesn’t necessarily reveal the underlying runtime and software components those applications depend on.


## **You can’t protect what you can’t see**


[OpenText™ Universal Discovery and CMDB](https://www.opentext.com/products/universal-discovery-and-cmdb) discovers, maps and manages configuration items across hybrid, network and multicloud environments. It provides software discovery and configuration data that can be shared across IT teams and tools.


Instead of relying on static or potentially outdated inventories, organizations can build a richer and more current picture of their IT estate and the relationships between its components. For security response, that changes the question from “Do we use PHP?” to:


“Where is PHP running in our environment, which business services depend on it, and which systems should we investigate first?”


## **Turn the CMDB into an operational map**


Discovery is only part of the answer. The real value comes when discovery data provides trusted configuration information that teams can use across operational processes. The CMDB[automatically collects, reconciles and manages configuration data](https://www.opentext.com/media/product-overview/opentext-universal-discovery-and-cmdb-po-en.pdf) covering infrastructure, services and their interdependencies.


That context matters during a critical vulnerability response. An infrastructure component doesn’t exist in isolation. It supports applications and services and depends on other configuration items. Service dependency mapping and impact analysis help operations teams assess the potential impact of a change before acting.


The CMDB becomes more than an inventory: a trusted foundation for faster, better-informed operational decisions. The faster an organization can establish where affected technology exists and understand its operational context, the faster it can move from investigation to remediation.


## **From visibility to automated remediation**


Knowing where a problem exists doesn’t fix it. Once potentially vulnerable infrastructure has been identified and the appropriate remediation determined, automation can help organizations move from insight to action at enterprise scale.


[OpenText™ Automation Center](https://www.opentext.com/products/automation-center) automates and orchestrates IT processes from a unified platform, including patching, remediation and compliance processes across complex IT environments.


The goal is a more connected lifecycle:


### **Discover → Understand → Prioritize → Remediate → Verify**


Your security team and scanning tools set the priority. OpenText helps with the rest: finding what’s affected, understanding the impact, applying the fix and confirming it worked.


Verification deserves its own attention. Some Linux distributions backport security fixes without changing the PHP version number, so teams need to confirm the runtime that’s actually executing, not just the package version or application state.


## **Less searching, more remediation**


One of the biggest costs in vulnerability response can be the time teams spend establishing their exposure before remediation can even begin.


Discovery and CMDB provide the visibility and configuration context. Automation brings orchestration to patching and remediation. Together, they shrink the gap between knowing that a vulnerability exists and being able to take controlled action against it.


That matters in increasingly distributed hybrid and multicloud environments, where manual inventories and disconnected operational processes can slow down response.


## **Preparing for the next critical vulnerability**


PHP2Shell will eventually disappear from the headlines. The underlying challenge will not.


The next critical vulnerability may affect a runtime, an operating system, a library or another widely deployed technology. When it arrives, teams will once again need to answer three questions quickly: Are we affected? Where are we affected? How quickly can we remediate?


The organizations best positioned to answer will be those that have already connected continuous discovery, trusted configuration data and IT automation.


Having the patch is important. Knowing exactly where to apply it, understanding the impact and being able to act at scale is what turns vulnerability information into operational resilience.
